data.note:
Note: Unblinded as cycloheximide (PubChem CID 6197, CHEMBL123292) - curated ChEMBL mechanism 80S Ribosome inhibitor, BBBC021 Protein synthesis - my call of Microtubule stabilizers was incorrect.

Reflection: Evidence was strongly misleading: tub_glcm_contrast z +55.8/+41.9 and tub_mean z +43.0/+35.6 with dose-response rho +1.0, plus microscopist report of bundled bright tubulin and atlas cosine similarity 0.935 to taxol and 0.914 to epothilone B (7/10 neighbors Microtubule stabilizers, mean 0.91) overwhelmed alternatives. I weighted intensity/texture z-scores as direct polymerization readout and discounted the atlas Protein degradation neighbors MG-132/ALLN (0.89) which were mechanistically closer to translation inhibition.

In hindsight Protein synthesis inhibition can produce secondary cytoskeletal stress phenotypes - contraction, reduced cell density/sparse monolayer, cortical actin spiking and apparent tubulin brightening due to cell shrinkage/compaction rather than true polymerization - that mimics stabilizer profiles in this DAPI/tubulin/actin assay. I failed to discriminate: I did not acquire an intermediate low dose to test early translation-specific features, nor request orthogonal validation (in vitro tubulin polymerization, phospho-H3 mitotic index, washout, or puromycin-incorporation assay) which the next-experiment I proposed would have tested.

Cycloheximide is a classic 80S ribosome protein synthesis inhibitor (reviewed as 80S-targeting strategy PMID:32151059), consistent with ChEMBL annotation, not a tubulin binder.

Lesson: do not equate high tubulin intensity + multinucleation n=1 well similarity to MoA; require functional discrimination between stabilizer and proteostasis/cytotoxic phenocopy.

reflection.text:
Unblinded as cycloheximide / cyclohexamide PubChem CID 6197, ChEMBL CHEMBL123292, annotated 80S Ribosome inhibitor e14,e15 - truth MOA Protein synthesis. Called Microtubule stabilizers at p=0.94 e12,e13 - incorrect. Review approved for same reason - also incorrect.

What the evidence got right:
- Dose-dependency and sign discrimination: tub_mean increased monotonically rho=+1.00 e8 from near-baseline at 0.05 uM e5 (frac_large_nucleus +4.1, tub not elevated) through onset at 0.5 uM e3 (tub_glcm_contrast +9.8) to huge effects at 15 uM e2 (tub_mean +35.6, tub_glcm_contrast +41.9) and 50 uM e4 (+43.0, +55.8). That correctly rules out microtubule destabilizers, which predict decrease. We also correctly deprioritized Actin disruptors to 1/10 neighbors e7 despite act_glcm_contrast +24.4 e2 appearing only at high doses as secondary effect.
- Phenotypic consistency: microscopist described bundled filaments, lower density e6, and dose_response showed concordant frac_multinucleate_proxy increase rho=+1.00 e9, nuc_solidity decrease rho=-1.00 e10 with extreme -41.1 at 50 uM e4, and cell_count decrease rho=-1.00 e11. Proliferation block and nuclear dysmorphology are consistent with global translation inhibition, but we read them as mitotic sequelae of stabilization.
- Atlas comparison e7 was faithfully reported: 7/10 Microtubule stabilizers vs 2/10 Protein degradation, 1/10 Actin disruptors. Protein degradation was the only proteostasis neighbor sampled, and we underweighted it at 0.03 e12. Hypothesis set did not contain Protein synthesis as distinct category; nearest proxy was protein degradation.

What misled us and why:
- Extreme effect size at saturating doses: first acquisitions were high dose 15 uM e2 and highest dose 50 uM e4 specifically to see strong phenotype. z-scores >+35 to +55 are rare and visually matched bundled microtubules e6, so we and the reviewer treated magnitude as evidence of direct target engagement. In retrospect, translation arrest at high concentration produces secondary cytoskeletal stabilization / accumulation and severe nuclear changes (nuc_solidity -41.1 e4, nuc_area -8.3 e3) that phenocopy stabilizers morphologically without direct tubulin binding. No paper in this run links protein synthesis inhibition to this tubulin morphology artifact: search for protein synthesis inhibitor actin tubulin morphology artifact returned 0 hits e18, so we had no literature anchor to counter the morphology.
- Nearest-neighbor comparison misled: atlas is morphology-only and at these high concentrations cycloheximide clusters with taxol-like stabilizers (taxol PubChem 36314 annotated Tubulin inhibitor e16). With only 2/10 proteostasis neighbors e7, distance in Cell Painting space dominated by shared bundled-tubulin, multinucleation, and low density features rather than mechanism.
- Acquisition choices: we sampled 4 doses with single replicate per dose e1-e5, spanning baseline/onset/saturating correctly, but all inference rested on single wells at 15 and 50 uM. Effect sizes were so extreme that replication was judged unlikely to reverse call - the reviewer explicitly stated this - but single-replicate design cannot estimate well-to-well variance for such pleiotropic stress phenotypes, and we had no orthogonal protein synthesis readout (e.g., puromycin incorporation) and no low-concentration proteostasis references to calibrate phenocopy threshold. Hypotheses were updated on same 4 wells e12.
- Post-unblinding literature e17 confirms the true mechanism is 80S ribosome inhibition, consistent with PMID 32151059, PMID 7201003 and PMID 1067615 describing cycloheximide-sensitive protein synthesis on 80S ribosomes. That was only looked up after submission e14-e17, so it could not inform the blinded call. We did not acquire an experiment that could distinguish stabilization via in vitro tubulin polymerization vs indirect stabilization after translation block, which was proposed as next experiment but would not have resolved this run.

Lesson: for extreme tubulin z-scores at cytotoxic high doses, require replication, lower-concentration profiling, and inclusion of protein synthesis inhibitors in reference atlas/hypothesis set before assigning 0.94 to a direct tubulin mechanism. Morphology alone is insufficient to separate direct microtubule stabilization from secondary stabilization downstream of 80S inhibition.
